newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair hopes IRA ceasefire heralds new era.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair hopes IRA ceasefire heralds new era.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair said on Saturday he hoped a new ceasefire announced by the IRA would herald a future free of violence and despair in Northern Ireland.
But Blair said there remained many problems ahead and the ceasefire, due to start at midday (1100 gmt) on Sunday, must be "genuine and unequivocal".

"There are still a lot of problems to be sorted out, but at least it gives us the chance of, and a hope for, a decent future for people in Northern Ireland, so that we don't have yet another generation of people growing up with violence and hatred and despair around them," Blair told reporters.
Blair said the Labour government, elected on May 1, would assess the operation of the truce with great care.

It restores a 1994 ceasefire declared by the Irish Republican Army but broken in February 1996 over the perceived intransigence of the then Conservative government, which refused to include the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein in peace talks.
The British and Irish governments, co-sponsors in the peace process, have said a new ceasefire must hold at least six weeks if Sinn Fein wants to enter the talks in September.

"The absolute essence is that it has to be a genuine and clear and unequivocal ceasefire. What I want to do is establish a process in which people can talk about a lasting political settlement in Northern Ireland and talk about it free from violence," Blair said.
Asked whether he could keep on board pro-British Unionist political parties, suspicious of Sinn Fein's ultimate aim of a united Ireland, Blair said;

"I hope very much that we can keep everyone in the talks process, because the thing that has transformed the situation is that everybody accepts -- and I hope that Sinn Fein will accept too -- that it is the consent of the people of Northern Ireland that must be the key thing."

Under new terms worked out by the new British and Irish governments aimed at unblocking a stalemate in negotiations which have been bogged down for a year, guerrillas will not have to disarm as a condition for the entry of their political wings to the talks.
Blair will on Monday hold talks with the leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, David Trimble, who believes that the plans to achieve IRA disarmament are too vague.
Trimble's party is threatening to oppose the plans at talks in Belfast next Wednesday.

Blair, whose Labour Party has a thumping 179-seat majority in the London parliament, has more freedom to manoeuvre in the peace process than his predecessor John Major who had to rely on the support of Unionist parties to keep his government in power in its final 12 months.

Blair said he wanted to secure a decent future for the people of Northern Ireland "where the politics...becomes about schools and hospitals and roads and all the rest of the things that people want to talk about, rather than the bitterness and hatred that have been there in the past".
